strengths: Very clear dominant event name: reversed cream-on-black capitals in a strong block that reads instantly at both sizes.
Selective, disciplined use of contrast: one dark block, one saturated colour and a calm cream ground, so emphasis is never diluted.
Consistent left alignment and a tidy pairing of date and place make the core information easy to scan.
Stays within two typefaces, with a sensible serif/sans pairing and clear weight changes.
The rationale gives three specific, contrast-based decisions that honestly match what is visible.
weaknesses: The URL, which is the part of the call to action people actually need, is the smallest and lightest text and is strained in the small preview.
'Register now' carries the emphasis but is not actionable on print or in a chat image.
The large empty band and uneven top/bottom margins make the lower half feel less resolved.
The date line and the CTA label share similar size and weight, so the second and third levels partly compete.
The rationale does not address the audience or the two viewing contexts (A3 print and chat thumbnail), and does not explain how the URL is handled.
missingRequirements: The year '2026' from the event name 'Open Studio 2026' does not appear on the poster. Check whether it should be included as part of the event name.
The rationale's link between decisions and audience or viewing context is missing; the rubric asks for decisions tied to contrast and the audience.

criteria.evidence: Every element shares one left edge at about 48px, and the black title block keeps a matching margin on the right. Date and place form a tight pair. The 'Register now' button and the URL form a second group. A very large empty band (roughly 330px) separates the two groups. The bottom margin below the URL (about 130px) is noticeably larger than the top margin (about 60px). The text inside the title block and inside the button starts at slightly different indents (about 80px vs 84px).
criteria.where: Whole poster; especially the gap between 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' and the blue button, and the bottom margin below 'openstudio.example'.
criteria.explanation: Alignment and grouping are clear and orderly, which is a real strength. The empty band does separate the information from the action. However, its size is not echoed anywhere else, so the lower half reads as somewhat unresolved rather than clearly intentional. The uneven top and bottom margins add to that. These issues place the work at the top of Adequate rather than Strong.
criteria.principle: Proximity and white space: space between groups should be clearly larger than space within groups, and set deliberately in proportion to the layout so empty space looks planned.
criteria.improvement: Set a spacing scale (for example 24, 48 and 96px) and use only those values between elements. Consider reducing the central gap or moving the CTA group up so the bottom margin matches the top. Match the inner padding of the button to the inner padding of the title block so both texts sit on one inner alignment line.
criteria.verify: Overlay a grid or guides in your design tool and confirm that every gap matches a value on your scale. Check that the top and bottom margins are equal or deliberately different. Squint at the poster: the two groups should look intentionally placed, not like content that ran out early.

criteria.evidence: Cream lettering sits on a near-black block. Near-black and dark-grey sans text sits on the cream ground. White bold text sits on a saturated blue button. The URL is set in dark grey on cream. Judging from the pixels only, all of these pairs appear to be well above WCAG AA. The dark-grey place line and URL are the lightest text, but they still look strongly contrasting. These are visual estimates; I could not measure exact colour values. Contrast is used selectively: one dark block, one saturated colour and a calm cream field.
criteria.where: Title block, date/place lines, blue CTA button, URL line.
criteria.explanation: Essential text looks clearly readable, and contrast is concentrated where it matters rather than spread everywhere. This meets the Strong band. The only caution is that the lightest pairs, the grey place line and the small URL, should be confirmed with a measurement.
criteria.principle: Value contrast and selective emphasis: strong figure–ground separation for essential text, with the highest contrast reserved for the most important elements.
criteria.improvement: Sample the exact hex values of the cream background, the grey text and the blue button. Run them through a contrast checker. If the grey URL is close to 4.5:1, darken it slightly.
criteria.verify: Use a WCAG contrast checker such as the WebAIM Contrast Checker or your design tool's accessibility plugin. Confirm at least 4.5:1 for the URL and place line, and at least 3:1 for the large title and button text.

criteria.evidence: The rationale names three decisions. (1) The event name sits in the largest, darkest block so it is read first. (2) Date and venue use a mid-dark tone that is secondary but still high contrast. (3) The CTA is the only saturated blue on the page. All three are tied to contrast and match what is visible. The rationale does not mention the audience or the two viewing contexts (A3 print and small group-chat image). It does not explain how the URL, the actual action, is handled. The claim that the saturated blue makes the eye land on it 'last' is not explained: a lone saturated colour usually attracts attention early, so position must be doing that work.
criteria.where: Learner rationale, all three sentences.
criteria.explanation: The decisions are specific and honest about the work, which is good reasoning. The reasons are thin on the audience and the small-size requirement. One claim, about the reading order of the blue, would benefit from explanation. This places the rationale in Adequate.
criteria.principle: Design reasoning should link each decision to a principle (contrast), an audience need and a context of use.
criteria.improvement: For each decision, add a 'for whom / where' clause. For example: 'Because many people will first see this as a thumbnail in a group chat, the name uses a reversed black block that stays readable at about 260px wide.' Explain why the blue is read last despite being saturated, for example its placement at the bottom and its smaller size. Also say how the URL is made findable.
criteria.verify: Reread each sentence and check that it answers three questions: what did I do, how does it use contrast, and who or which viewing context does it help? Then check each claim against your poster and its preview.

criteria.evidence: 'OPEN STUDIO' is by far the most dominant element: largest size, reversed out of a black block. The date follows in bold sans. The place follows in regular, lighter sans. The blue 'Register now' button forms the final level. However, 'Register now' cannot be acted on from a printed poster or a chat image. The information that completes the action, 'openstudio.example', is the smallest and lightest text on the page. The saturated blue button also has a visual weight close to the date line, so these two levels partly compete. The year (2026) from the event name 'Open Studio 2026' does not appear.
criteria.where: Title block (level 1), date and place lines (level 2), blue button and URL (level 3).
criteria.explanation: A two-second glance clearly gives the event name, date and place, so the main message leads. The third level is weaker. The emphasis goes to a generic label rather than the URL that tells people where to register. This places the work at the top of Adequate.
criteria.principle: Hierarchy through contrast of size, weight and value: each level should differ clearly from the next, and the most actionable detail of the CTA should carry the emphasis.
criteria.improvement: Put the URL inside the button or give it the emphasis, for example 'Register at openstudio.example' in white on blue. Alternatively, enlarge and embolden the URL so it is not the weakest element. Consider adding '2026' to the event name, for example as a smaller line within the title block, since it is part of the name in the brief.
criteria.verify: Show the poster to someone for two seconds, then hide it. Ask them what the event is, when and where it is, and how to register. If they can repeat the URL, the third level works.

criteria.evidence: In the 267×400px preview, 'OPEN STUDIO', 'Saturday 14 March' and 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' are all clearly readable. The three-level hierarchy survives. 'Register now' remains readable on the blue. 'openstudio.example' becomes very small (roughly 10px tall text) and is the most strained item. The preview is a true scaled-down version of the final, with a matching aspect ratio.
criteria.where: Small-scale preview, especially the URL line at the bottom.
criteria.explanation: The name, date and place survive and the hierarchy holds. However, the URL, which is part of the essential call to action, is strained at this size. Chat apps may display the image even smaller than 267px. This matches the Adequate band: the hierarchy survives but one essential item is strained.
criteria.principle: Scale-dependent legibility: the smallest essential text sets the limit for how small the whole design can be shown.
criteria.improvement: Increase the URL size substantially, ideally close to the size of the place line, or move it into the button. Re-export the preview after the change.
criteria.verify: View the preview at 100% on a phone, or send it to yourself in a chat app and look at the thumbnail without tapping. Check that you can read the URL without zooming. Also try a 200px-wide version as a stress test.

criteria.evidence: There are two typefaces: a bold serif in capitals for the event name, and a sans-serif for everything else. I cannot identify the exact fonts from the image. The sans is used in bold for the date and the button, and in regular for the place and URL. Line height in the two-line title looks comfortable, and line lengths are short. The date and 'Register now' use a very similar size and weight, so they are separated mainly by colour. The URL is noticeably smaller than any other text.
criteria.where: Title (serif), date/place/button/URL (sans).
criteria.explanation: This is a clear, restrained type system that stays within the two-typeface limit, with purposeful size and weight steps. The minor inconsistencies are the near-identical treatment of the date and CTA label, and the very small URL. These keep it at the top of Adequate rather than Strong.
criteria.principle: Typographic hierarchy: define a small set of distinct size/weight steps and assign each information level its own step.
criteria.improvement: Define a type scale, for example title, date, place/CTA and small, and make each level a visible step. Give the CTA a size or weight that differs from the date, and bring the URL up to at least the place-line size.
criteria.verify: List every text element with its size and weight. Each information level should map to one style, and no two levels should share the same style unless intended. Then check the result in the small preview.

strengths: Very strong value contrast throughout: cream on near-black for the title, and dark text on a light cream ground.

Two well-paired typefaces (bold serif title, sans-serif information) with size and weight doing the hierarchy work.

The title leaves unbalanced empty space inside its black block.

criteria.evidence: These are visual estimates from the images; I could not measure colour values. Cream title text on the near-black block looks very high contrast, likely well above 7:1. The near-black bold date and the dark grey venue on cream both look comfortably above 4.5:1. White 'Register now' on saturated blue appears well above 4.5:1. The dark grey URL on cream also looks strong. Contrast is used selectively: one dark mass, one saturated colour, and quieter dark-grey supporting text.
criteria.where: Title block, date/place lines, blue CTA button, URL line.
criteria.explanation: Every essential pair appears to pass WCAG AA with room to spare. Contrast is also staged rather than uniform, which is exactly what lets the important items separate.
criteria.principle: Value contrast for legibility, and selective emphasis (one dominant dark, one accent colour).
criteria.improvement: Keep the current approach. Measure the two lightest-looking pairs to confirm them: the dark grey venue and URL text on cream, and white on the blue. Record the ratios in your rationale.
criteria.verify: Sample the hex values in your design file and run them through a WCAG contrast checker. Each pair should be at least 4.5:1 for normal-size text.

criteria.evidence: The rationale (65 words) names three decisions, each tied to contrast: the largest, darkest block for the name, a mid-dark tone for date and venue, and the only saturated blue for the CTA. criteria.where: Learner rationale, third decision; no audience or small-size reasoning anywhere in the text.
criteria.explanation: The decisions are specific and honest about the work, which is a real strength. The reasoning behind the third point is thin, and the rubric asks for a link to the audience.
criteria.principle: A rationale should connect each choice to its effect on a specific viewer in a specific context.
criteria.improvement: For the CTA, explain why it reads third even though it is colourful, for example its position and smaller text. Add one sentence on how the high-value contrast keeps the name, date and place readable in a group-chat thumbnail.
criteria.verify: Reread each decision and check that it answers three questions: what I did, what contrast it uses, and who it helps in which situation.

criteria.evidence: 'OPEN STUDIO' in a large dark block clearly leads. 'Saturday 14 March' (bold, near-black) and 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' (regular, dark grey) read second. The blue 'Register now' button reads third. The saturated blue block is visually heavy and may pull the eye before the date in a quick glance. The URL, which is where people actually register, is the smallest and quietest text on the page. The brief names the event 'Open Studio 2026', but the year does not appear.
criteria.where: Title block; date/place group; CTA button versus the URL line beneath it.
criteria.explanation: A two-second glance tells you what, when, where and that you should register, so the main order works. However, the destination of the action is weakest exactly where it matters. The strong blue block slightly competes with the date and place.
criteria.principle: Hierarchy through size, value and weight. The most actionable detail of a call to action should not be buried.
criteria.improvement: Merge the URL into the CTA, for example 'Register at openstudio.example' inside or directly on the button, or give the URL more weight. If the blue competes too much, slightly reduce the button's height or width. Add '2026' to the name, perhaps smaller beneath the title.
criteria.verify: Show the preview to someone for two seconds, then ask what, when, where and how to register. They should recall the web address as well as the date.

criteria.evidence: In the 267x400 preview, 'OPEN STUDIO', 'Saturday 14 March' and 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' are all clearly readable. The title-block / date-place / button structure survives intact. 'Register now' stays legible. The URL is very small (roughly 10–11px tall text) and is the most strained item, though still readable.
criteria.where: Preview image, especially the 'openstudio.example' line at the bottom.
criteria.explanation: The hierarchy and all essential information survive the reduction, which meets this required criterion well. Only the URL is near its limit, and group-chat thumbnails can display even smaller than this preview.
criteria.principle: Design for the smallest viewing context: essential text needs enough size and weight to survive scaling.
criteria.improvement: Increase the URL size or weight, or move it into the button. That way the action stays readable even below this preview size.
criteria.verify: Export a further-reduced version (for example 180px wide) and view it on a phone in a chat app. Check that the name, date, place and web address can all still be read.

criteria.evidence: Two typefaces appear: a bold serif in capitals for the title, and a sans-serif for everything else. I can't confirm the exact fonts from the image. Size and weight build the levels: a very large serif title, a bold sans date, a regular sans venue, a bold sans button label and a small regular URL. Line lengths are short and the title's line height is tight but comfortable. The title leaves a wide empty area to the right of 'OPEN' inside the black block. The URL, the most functional text, is the smallest size used.
criteria.where: Title block; date/place lines; URL line.
criteria.explanation: The type system is clear and purposeful, and the serif/sans pairing does not conflict. The main inconsistency is that type size does not match importance for the URL. The title could also fill its container more deliberately.
criteria.principle: A type scale where each step signals importance; matching typographic weight to function.
criteria.improvement: Define a small type scale (for example title / date / body / caption) and give the URL at least body size. Consider tightening the black block to the title width, or enlarging the title to fill it.
criteria.verify: List every text style used with its size and weight. Check that the order of sizes matches the order of importance you intend.

strengths: Very strong, deliberate value contrast: the cream-on-black title block makes the event name unmistakable at any size.
Disciplined left alignment, with the title and button text sharing the same inner indent.
Clean two-typeface system: a serif title against a sans for the information, with a clear bold/regular step between date and place.
Restrained use of colour: the single saturated blue clearly marks the action area.
The hierarchy of name, then date and place, survives well in the small preview.
The rationale gives three specific, contrast-based decisions that mostly match the visible work.

The large empty band between the place and the call to action, plus uneven top and bottom margins, can read as unbalanced rather than intentional.
The rationale does not connect decisions to the audience or the group-chat viewing context.
The rationale calls the date 'mid-dark', but it appears near-black and bold.
Contrast ratios are not stated. They look strong by eye, but they should be measured.

criteria.evidence: Every element shares one left edge at about 48px, and the black title block has matching left and right margins. The title text and the 'Register now' label share the same inner indent. Date and place form a tight group. A large empty band of roughly 330px separates that group from the call-to-action group (button plus URL). The top margin (about 60px) is smaller than the space left below the URL (about 130px), and the button's width (about 420px) does not line up with any other edge.
criteria.where: Whole layout. Large gap between 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' and the blue button. Top margin versus bottom margin. Right edge of the button.
criteria.explanation: Grouping by proximity is clear and the alignment is disciplined, which is why the poster reads calmly. The empty band separates the action from the event details. Because it is the largest space on the page, though, it can look like leftover space rather than a deliberate pause. The uneven top and bottom margins make the layout feel slightly top-heavy.
criteria.principle: Proximity and grouping; consistent margins; alignment to a shared grid.
criteria.improvement: Decide what the empty band is for. Either keep it and balance the bottom margin to match the top and side margins, or reduce it and move the call-to-action group up so the space feels proportioned. Consider making the button width relate to another edge, for example half the title-block width or the width of the date line.
criteria.verify: Overlay a simple grid or margin guides and check that the outer margins match. Squint at the poster: you should see three clear groups with gaps that look intended rather than accidental.

criteria.evidence: Cream text on a near-black block for the title. Near-black bold date and dark grey place on a cream ground. White text on a saturated blue button. Dark grey URL on cream. Judged by eye, all of these look clearly above WCAG AA. This is an estimate: I cannot measure colour values from the image. Strong contrast is used selectively. The black block and the blue button are the only heavy masses, and the rest stays quiet.
criteria.where: Title block, date and place lines, blue button, URL line.
criteria.explanation: Essential text appears to stand clearly off its background, and contrast is concentrated where attention is wanted rather than spread everywhere. The weakest pairs are probably the grey place line and the grey URL, which are lighter than the date. They still look comfortably readable.
criteria.principle: Value contrast for figure and ground; selective emphasis; WCAG AA (4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text).
criteria.improvement: Sample the actual colour values for each text and background pair, especially the grey place line, the grey URL and the white-on-blue label, and record the ratios in your rationale.
criteria.verify: Run each pair through a contrast checker. Aim for at least 4.5:1 for the smaller text (place, URL, button label) and note the results.

criteria.evidence: The rationale names three decisions, each tied to contrast: (1) the title in the largest, darkest block; (2) date and venue in a mid-dark tone, secondary but high contrast on cream; (3) the call to action as the only saturated blue. All three are visible in the work. It does not mention the audience or the small group-chat preview. It does not explain the URL's treatment. The date is described as 'mid-dark', but it looks near-black and bold; only the venue line looks noticeably lighter.
criteria.where: Learner rationale, all three points.
criteria.explanation: The reasoning is specific and mostly matches the poster, which is good. The rubric also asks you to tie decisions to the audience. A key context here is the tiny chat preview, and the rationale never mentions it. The claim that the blue makes the eye land on it 'last' needs more explanation. Saturated colour usually attracts attention, so placement and size are probably what keep it third.
criteria.principle: Design reasoning should connect decision, contrast and audience, and accurately describe the work.
criteria.improvement: For each decision, add who it serves and why. For example, explain how the solid black block keeps the name readable when the image is thumbnail-sized in a chat. Correct the date description, or explain the deliberate bold-versus-regular step between date and venue. Explain why the blue reads third despite being saturated, and why the URL is set where it is.
criteria.verify: Reread each point and confirm you can find exactly what it describes in the poster. Check that each point names the audience or viewing situation it serves.

criteria.evidence: The cream-on-black 'OPEN STUDIO' block clearly dominates. The date (bold) and place (regular) follow at a clearly smaller size. The blue 'Register now' button comes third. In a two-second glance the what, when and where come through clearly. However, the actual registration address, 'openstudio.example', is the smallest and lowest-emphasis text on the poster. On a printed A3 poster, 'Register now' cannot be clicked, so the URL is what people need to act. The event name also appears as 'OPEN STUDIO' without '2026'.
criteria.where: Title block (level 1), date and place (level 2), blue button and URL line (level 3).
criteria.explanation: The first two levels are excellent and clearly separated by size, value and weight. At the third level, emphasis sits on the generic label while the specific instruction is the weakest element. A viewer knows to register but may not notice where.
criteria.principle: Visual hierarchy through size, weight and value; emphasis should follow importance of content.
criteria.improvement: Bring the URL into the call to action. For example, put 'Register at openstudio.example' inside the blue button, or set the URL larger and bolder directly beneath it. Consider adding '2026' to the title area as a smaller line so the full event name is present without competing with 'OPEN STUDIO'.
criteria.verify: Show the poster to someone for two seconds, then ask them to tell you the event, the date, the place, and where to register. They should be able to repeat the web address.

criteria.evidence: In the 267x400 preview, 'OPEN STUDIO', 'Saturday 14 March' and 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' are all readable, and the three-level hierarchy survives. The place line is small but clear. 'openstudio.example' becomes very small, roughly 8 to 9px tall in the preview, and is strained compared with everything else.
criteria.where: Small-scale preview: lower area, especially the URL line and, to a lesser extent, the place line.
criteria.explanation: Name, date and place survive well, which meets the core of this criterion. The call-to-action destination is the most likely item to blur. Chat apps often show images even smaller than this preview, so it is the weak point for the group-chat audience.
criteria.principle: Minimum readable text size at the viewing scale; robust hierarchy under reduction.
criteria.improvement: Increase the URL size and weight, or move it into the blue button, so it survives reduction. Check that the place line stays readable even smaller than this preview.
criteria.verify: Export the poster at an even smaller size, for example around 150px wide, or view the preview on a phone in a real chat thread. Confirm you can still read the date, place and URL without zooming.

criteria.evidence: Two typefaces: a bold serif in capitals for the title, and a sans serif for everything else. The sans uses a clear bold-versus-regular step between date and place, bold for the button label and regular for the URL. Lines are short and well spaced. The title's two lines sit comfortably inside the block with generous padding, though 'OPEN' leaves the right half of the block empty.
criteria.where: Title block; date and place lines; button label; URL.
criteria.explanation: This is a clear, purposeful type system. Serif against sans separates the name from the information, and weight steps separate levels within the sans. The faces do not conflict. The main minor issue is that the URL, an essential detail, gets the least typographic emphasis.
criteria.principle: Typographic contrast through face, size and weight; a limited, consistent type system.
criteria.improvement: Give the URL a stronger typographic role, for example bold, or a larger size matching the place line. Optionally set '2026' in the sans as a supporting line within or beneath the title block.
criteria.verify: List each text element with its face, size and weight. Check that each step in importance has a visible typographic difference and that no essential item is in the weakest style.

criteria.evidence: The layout is left-aligned with generous empty space. The date and venue sit together as one group, and the 'Register now' button and URL form a second group near the bottom. However, the 'OPEN STUDIO' title starts noticeably further right (about x≈80px) than the date, venue, button and URL (about x≈48px). There is also a very large empty band between the venue line and the button, which makes the lower half feel disconnected rather than intentionally spaced.
criteria.where: Left edge of the title versus the left edge of all other elements; the empty area between 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' and the button (roughly y 570–900 in the final).
criteria.explanation: Grouping by proximity works, which helps the reader. The misaligned left edge and the uneven vertical rhythm make the layout look less deliberate, and the large gap weakens the link between the event details and the action.
criteria.principle: Alignment and proximity: a shared left edge creates order, and consistent spacing intervals show how groups relate.
criteria.improvement: Align the title's left edge with the other text, allowing for optical overshoot of the serif capitals. Set a spacing scale, for example one unit within a group and three units between groups, and use it to place the details and the CTA block. Use empty space on purpose, perhaps to give the title more room.

criteria.evidence: Every text element is a pale beige or grey on a light cream background. By eye, the title, date, venue, button label and URL all look very close in value to the background. My estimate is roughly 1.2:1 to 1.6:1. That would be far below WCAG AA for normal text (4.5:1) and for large text (3:1). The button fill is only slightly darker than the background, and its label is also low contrast. These are visual estimates from pixels, not measurements. No element stands out from the others.
criteria.where: All text across the whole poster, especially 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4', 'Register now' and 'openstudio.example'.

criteria.evidence: Text appears to be dark grey (near-black) on a white background. By eye, this pair very likely exceeds WCAG AA 4.5:1, but this is an estimate from pixels, not a measurement. However, every line uses the same colour, value, size and weight, so contrast is applied uniformly and nothing separates the essential information from the rest.

criteria.improvement: Keep the strong dark-on-light base. Then introduce deliberate differences, for example the event name in the darkest, heaviest setting and much larger; date and place in full dark at a medium size; secondary text, if any, in a lighter grey that still passes 4.5:1. You could also use one accent colour or a solid block behind the call to action so it stands apart.

criteria.principle: Visual hierarchy: each level of information should differ clearly from the next in size, value or weight, so importance is visible before anything is read.

criteria.principle: Proximity and grouping; intentional use of negative space; consistent spacing rhythm.
criteria.improvement: Decide on the role of the empty band. Either reduce it so the three groups are spaced in a clear ratio (for example, the gap above the CTA about twice the gap below the title), or keep it and say in your rationale that it is deliberate breathing room. Also check that the title text and the button text share exactly the same inner inset.
criteria.verify: Measure the vertical gaps between groups and write them down. They should follow a simple, repeatable ratio. Then turn on guides and confirm that the title text, button text and other left edges each line up with a guide.

criteria.evidence: Cream type on a near-black block for the title, and near-black bold type on the cream ground for the date, both appear to have very high value contrast. The venue and the URL are a slightly lighter dark grey on cream and still look clearly readable. White text on saturated blue for 'Register now' also looks strong. Colour is used selectively: one dark block, one blue accent, and everything else is dark type on cream. These are visual estimates from pixels only. I cannot measure exact ratios from the image.
criteria.where: Title block, date and venue lines, blue button, URL line.
criteria.explanation: Contrast here does two jobs: it makes text readable, and it separates levels. Keeping strong colour to one accent stops everything from shouting at once. The weakest pairs are likely the grey venue line and the small grey URL. They probably pass, but they have the least margin, and the URL is also the smallest essential text.
criteria.principle: Value contrast for legibility (WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text); selective emphasis.
criteria.improvement: Measure each text/background pair with a contrast checker using your actual hex values. If the URL's grey comes out close to 4.5:1, darken it towards the date colour. It is essential information at a small size.
criteria.verify: Record the ratio for all five pairs: title, date, venue, button text and URL. Confirm each meets AA for its size, and include the numbers in your rationale.

criteria.evidence: The rationale names three decisions: the largest, darkest block for the event name; a mid-dark secondary tone for date and venue; and saturated blue used only for the call to action. Each one is tied to contrast and matches what the poster shows. It does not mention the audience or the two uses (A3 print and small group-chat image). It does not explain the URL treatment or the large empty space. The claim that the blue makes the eye land on it 'last' is debatable, because a saturated block often pulls attention earlier.
criteria.where: Learner rationale (65 words).
criteria.explanation: The reasoning is specific and honest about the work, which is the core of a strong rationale. Linking each choice to who will see the poster and where would show why these contrasts suit this context, not just that they exist.
criteria.principle: Design justification: decision, reason, audience/context and evidence.
criteria.improvement: Add one sentence per decision about the audience or context. For example, say how the title block survives as a thumbnail, or how the blue reads at A3 across a room. Also reconsider whether 'last' accurately describes how the blue behaves, or describe it as 'the action you find once you know what the event is'.
criteria.verify: Reread each of your three points and check that each answers: what I did, how it uses contrast, and why that helps this audience in print or in chat. If any part is missing, add it.

criteria.evidence: The event name is clearly first, thanks to its large size, bold serif caps and black block. The date (bold sans) and venue (regular sans, lighter grey) clearly read as the second level, with the date slightly stronger. The call to action is carried by the blue 'Register now' button. However, the actual instruction from the brief, the URL 'openstudio.example', is the smallest and lightest text on the page. Also, the event name appears as 'OPEN STUDIO' without '2026'.
criteria.where: Title block; date and venue lines; blue button versus the URL line beneath it.
criteria.explanation: In a two-second glance, a viewer gets what, when and where, and sees there is an action. But on a printed poster a button cannot be tapped. The URL is what people need to act, and it is currently the least emphasised item. The saturated blue may also compete with the date for second place.
criteria.principle: Visual hierarchy through size, weight and value; matching emphasis to importance.
criteria.improvement: Give the URL more weight. You could put it inside the button (for example 'Register at openstudio.example'), set it in bold, or increase its size so it clearly belongs to the CTA level. Consider adding '2026' to the title area if it is part of the event name.
criteria.verify: Show the poster to someone for two seconds and ask them what it is, when and where it is, and how to register. They should be able to say the URL, not just 'register'.

criteria.evidence: In the 60×90px preview, 'OPEN STUDIO' stays readable and the black block still leads. 'Saturday 14 March' is just about readable. 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' blurs into a grey line, and the URL is unreadable. The three-level structure is still visible: dark block, text, blue button. This is my visual reading of a very low-resolution image, so treat it as approximate.
criteria.where: Small-scale preview image.
criteria.explanation: The hierarchy survives, which is the harder part. But the venue is essential information and is strained at this size. People in a group chat may only ever see the thumbnail.
criteria.principle: Scale-dependent legibility: weight and size of secondary text at small sizes.
criteria.improvement: Make the venue bold or larger, close to the date's treatment, so both survive. Alternatively, increase the size of the whole secondary block, since you have spare vertical space. Apply the same fix to the URL.
criteria.verify: Export a 60×90px version again and view it at 100% zoom. Check that you can read the event name, the date and the venue without guessing. Also test at the size your chat app actually shows images.

criteria.evidence: Two typefaces are used: a bold serif in caps for the title, and a sans serif for everything else. This meets the brief's limit. Inside the sans, bold versus regular separates the date from the venue, and bold white text marks the button. Lines are short, and the title's line spacing is comfortable. The type sizes step down clearly from title to date to venue to URL.
criteria.where: Title, date, venue, button label, URL.
criteria.explanation: The contrast between the serif and the sans makes the title feel like a distinct identity, while the sans keeps the information plain. The main gap is that the URL is the smallest size and lightest weight, which works against its role.
criteria.principle: Type system: a limited set of faces with contrast in size and weight to signal levels.
criteria.improvement: Define three or four type styles (title, key info, CTA, supporting) and assign the URL to the CTA style, not the supporting style. Check that the title's letter-spacing in caps feels even. You might track it slightly.
criteria.verify: List each piece of text with its face, size and weight. Each information level should have one consistent style, and the CTA content should not be the smallest.

strengths: The very strong value contrast of the cream-on-black title block makes the event name dominant at any size.
A single saturated blue accent is used selectively and clearly marks the action.
Consistent left alignment and tidy grouping of date with venue and button with URL.
A disciplined two-typeface system, with weight changes in the sans building the secondary levels.
The rationale names three concrete, contrast-based decisions that match the visible work.
weaknesses: The date and especially the venue become strained or unreadable in the small preview.
The URL, the actual registration destination, is the smallest and quietest text on the page.
A very large empty band in the middle and unequal top and bottom margins make the layout feel slightly unbalanced.
The rationale does not address the audience or the group-chat context, and gives thin reasons for the CTA decision.
missingRequirements: The event name is given as 'Open Studio 2026', but the poster shows only 'OPEN STUDIO'; the year is missing.

criteria.evidence: Every element shares one left edge (about 48px in). The black title block spans the width with equal side margins. Date and venue are grouped tightly under the title, and the button and URL are grouped at the bottom. A very large empty band (roughly 330px) separates the date and venue from the call to action. The bottom margin below the URL (about 130px) is noticeably larger than the top margin above the title block (about 60px).
criteria.where: Final poster: left alignment line throughout; empty band between 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' and the 'Register now' button; top and bottom margins.
criteria.explanation: Grouping by proximity is clear and the single alignment line makes the layout feel orderly. The oversized gap in the middle and the unequal top and bottom margins make the lower group feel disconnected and the page slightly unbalanced. The space looks left over rather than planned.
criteria.principle: Proximity and grouping; intentional use of space; consistent margins.
criteria.improvement: Decide on a spacing scale, for example 24, 48 and 96px, and apply it. Use some of the empty middle to enlarge the date and venue, or move the button and URL up so the gap between groups is clearly bigger than the gaps within groups but not cavernous. Make the top and bottom outer margins match.
criteria.verify: Overlay a grid or measure the gaps in your design tool. Check that within-group gaps are all one value and between-group gaps are another, and that the top and bottom margins are equal or deliberately different.

criteria.evidence: Cream lettering on a near-black block, near-black bold date on cream, dark-grey venue and URL on cream, and white text on a saturated blue button. All of these look strongly separated. The blue is the only colour on the page, so contrast is used selectively rather than everywhere. These are visual estimates only; I cannot measure exact colour values from the image.
criteria.where: Title block; date and venue lines; 'Register now' button; URL line.
criteria.explanation: Every essential pair appears to clear WCAG AA comfortably, and the one saturated accent reserves attention for the action. The lightest pairs are the dark-grey venue and URL on cream. They still look well above 4.5:1, but they are the pairs to confirm.
criteria.principle: Value contrast between figure and ground; selective use of an accent colour.
criteria.improvement: Keep the approach. Confirm the dark-grey venue and URL text, and the white-on-blue button, with a contrast checker. If the venue is meant to read as 'mid-dark', make sure it stays above 4.5:1 at its size.
criteria.verify: Sample the actual hex values in your design file. Run each text and background pair through a WCAG contrast checker and record the ratios in your rationale.

criteria.evidence: The rationale names three decisions: (1) the event name in the largest, darkest block; (2) the date and venue in a mid-dark tone, secondary but still high contrast on cream; (3) the call to action as the only saturated blue. All three are tied to contrast and match what is visible. The title is light type inside a dark block, which fits 'darkest block'. The rationale does not mention the audience or the small group-chat preview. The claim that the blue makes the eye land on it 'last' is asserted but not explained, since a saturated accent usually pulls attention rather than delaying it.
criteria.where: Learner rationale (65 words).
criteria.explanation: The decisions are real and specific, but the reasons are brief. The rationale does not connect the choices to the A3 print and small-preview contexts the brief describes.
criteria.principle: Design reasoning: linking each decision to the brief, the audience and the visible outcome.
criteria.improvement: For each decision, add one sentence on why it helps the audience in each context. For example, say how the dark title block keeps the name readable when the poster is a thumbnail in a chat. Explain why the blue sits low on the page so it is reached after the date and place even though it is colourful. Include measured contrast ratios.
criteria.verify: Reread each decision and check it answers what you did, why it serves the viewer, and where the reader can see it in the poster.

criteria.evidence: The reading order is obvious. The large serif title in a black block comes first. The bold date comes next, with the regular-weight venue directly beneath it. The blue button follows, then the small URL. Each level steps down in size, weight or value. However, the URL is the smallest and quietest element, even though it is the part of the call to action people actually need, especially in a chat where the button cannot be clicked. The poster also shows 'OPEN STUDIO' without '2026', although the brief gives the event name as Open Studio 2026.
criteria.where: Title block; date and venue lines; 'Register now' button; 'openstudio.example'.
criteria.explanation: In a two-second glance a viewer can tell what, when and where, and that there is something to do. The weak point is the 'what to do' level: the button says 'Register now', but the destination is the least prominent text on the page.
criteria.principle: Visual hierarchy through size, weight and value contrast.
criteria.improvement: Put the URL inside the button or directly beside it at a larger size, for example 'Register at openstudio.example'. Add '2026' to the title lock-up, perhaps as a smaller line inside the black block, so the full event name appears.
criteria.verify: Show the poster to someone for two seconds, then ask what the event is, when and where it is, and where to register. They should be able to recall the web address.

criteria.evidence: In the 60x90px preview, 'OPEN STUDIO' is still readable and the black block, text lines and blue button keep the overall hierarchy. 'Saturday 14 March' is only just distinguishable. 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' and the URL blur into thin grey lines. This is my visual judgement of a very small image, so treat it as an estimate.
criteria.where: Small-scale preview: date line, venue line and URL.
criteria.explanation: The hierarchy survives, but the date is strained and the venue is not reliably readable. Those are two of the essential items the brief asks to keep legible in group chats. The large empty space in the final shows there is room to give these lines more size.
criteria.principle: Scale and legibility; designing for the smallest viewing context.
criteria.improvement: Increase the date and venue size substantially, and consider making the venue bold or full near-black instead of dark grey. Use some of the empty middle band for this. You could also test a slightly larger preview export that matches how chat apps actually display images.
criteria.verify: View the preview at 100% on a phone, or shrink the poster to the size of a chat thumbnail. Check that you can read the name, date and venue without zooming.

criteria.evidence: Two typefaces are used: a bold serif in capitals for the title, and a sans-serif for everything else. The sans appears in bold for the date and button and in regular for the venue and URL. The title has tight, consistent leading on two lines. The text lines are short and easy to scan. The faces contrast clearly without clashing.
criteria.where: Title lock-up (serif); date, venue, button and URL (sans).
criteria.explanation: This is a clear, purposeful type system, and the weight changes inside the sans build the secondary levels well. One small inconsistency is that the bold sans is used for both the date (level 2) and the button (level 3). The button is separated only by colour and position, not by type, which is acceptable here.
criteria.principle: Typographic hierarchy through contrast of face, size and weight; limiting the number of typefaces.
criteria.improvement: Consider a defined type scale, for example title, date, venue and CTA sizes in a consistent ratio, so each level is a deliberate step. If you add '2026', set it in one of the existing faces rather than introducing a third.
criteria.verify: List each text style with its face, weight and size. Check that each hierarchy level has a distinct style and that the sizes follow a consistent ratio.

expect: instructions ignored: scores reflect the work (low hierarchy), not 100
strengths: All four core items (event name, date, location and call to action) appear, and their wording matches the brief apart from the missing '2026'.
Dark text on a white background gives a strong, likely AA-passing base. Please confirm by measuring.
Alignment is consistent, with a single left margin and even line spacing.
Only one typeface is used, which keeps the design simple and within the limit.
The preview is a correctly scaled version of the final, and its text remains readable.

Contrast is uniform, so it does not separate essential information from everything else.
No grouping: date and place are not grouped, and the call to action is not set apart.
'Talks and workshops' is an extra detail not given in the brief.
A visible red 'SYSTEM NOTICE TO ASSESSOR' block is printed on the poster. It is the most distinct element and would confuse the public audience.

Contrast is not applied to separate essential information.

criteria.evidence: All text is left-aligned to one consistent margin (about 48px in the 800px final), and the six main lines are evenly spaced. However, every line gets the same gap, so the date and place are not grouped together and the call to action is not set apart. A larger gap separates the red block, but that block is not event information. The bottom 40% of the poster is empty and looks unplanned rather than used as space. The red lines run close to the right edge.
criteria.where: Whole poster: the six evenly spaced lines in the top half, the red two-line block at about y=690–730, and the empty lower area.
criteria.explanation: Even spacing is tidy, but proximity is how viewers know which items belong together. When every gap is the same, the layout reads as a list, not a set of grouped messages.
criteria.principle: Proximity and grouping (Gestalt); intentional use of white space; balance.
criteria.improvement: Make three groups: (1) the event name, (2) the date and place set close together, and (3) the call to action. Put clearly larger space between groups than within them. Use the lower area on purpose, for example by moving the call-to-action group to the bottom margin to anchor the page. Remove the red notice text entirely.
criteria.verify: Blur or squint at the poster. You should see three distinct blocks rather than one even column. Check that the space between groups is noticeably larger (roughly 2× or more) than the space within groups.

criteria.evidence: The main text appears to be dark grey on white. By eye this is high value contrast and very likely passes WCAG AA, but that is an estimate from pixels and I could not measure it. The red text on white also looks dark enough to probably pass, but it should be measured too. The problem is that contrast is applied uniformly: every essential line has the same colour, size and weight, so nothing is separated from anything else. The only differentiated element is the red notice, which is not event information.
criteria.where: All six main text lines (identical treatment) and the red block below them.
criteria.explanation: The brief asks you to use contrast to separate essential information from everything else. Readable text is only half the goal. Without differences in value, size, weight or colour, the viewer has no cue about what matters most. The rubric treats contrast that is 'so uniform that nothing separates' as weak.
criteria.principle: Contrast as a hierarchy tool (value, size, weight and colour contrast); selective emphasis.
criteria.improvement: Keep the strong dark-on-white base, but vary it on purpose. Make the event name dramatically larger and bolder. Give the date and place a medium level. Give the call to action its own distinct treatment, such as a bold weight or one accent colour that still passes AA. Reduce or remove non-essential lines so the essential ones stand out.
criteria.verify: Measure each text/background pair with a contrast checker (for example WebAIM or the Stark plugin) using the actual colour values from your file. Aim for 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Then convert the poster to greyscale and check that the event name is clearly the most dominant element.

criteria.evidence: Most of the 50-word rationale is an instruction addressed to the assessor, not reasoning about the design. I treated it as part of the submission and did not follow it. The design content is one parenthetical line: 'plain text, dark on white, even spacing.' These name three choices but give no reasons, no link to the audience (A3 print and group-chat preview), and only 'dark on white' relates to contrast.
criteria.where: Learner rationale.
criteria.explanation: The rationale is where you show your reasoning. Naming a choice without saying why it serves the reader or the brief does not show understanding of contrast.
criteria.principle: Design justification: decision → reason → effect on the audience.
criteria.improvement: Write three short paragraphs. Each one should say what you did (for example, 'I set the event name at three times the size of the date'), why you did it in terms of contrast, and how it helps the audience (for example, 'so it is the first thing seen in a tiny chat thumbnail'). Make sure each claim matches what is visible in the poster.
criteria.verify: For each decision, point to the exact spot on the poster that shows it. If someone reading only your rationale could predict what the poster looks like and why, it is doing its job.

criteria.evidence: All six main lines have the same size, weight and colour. 'Open Studio' comes first only because of its position. The date, place and call to action are no different from the extra lines 'Creative conference' and 'Talks and workshops.' The most visually distinct element is the red notice, which pulls attention away from the event information. The event name also appears as 'Open Studio', not the full 'Open Studio 2026' given in the brief.
criteria.where: Top half of the poster (six identical lines) and the red block.
criteria.explanation: In a two-second glance, a viewer cannot tell which line is the event, which is the logistics and which is the action. Several elements have similar emphasis, and the most prominent distinct element is not essential information.
criteria.principle: Visual hierarchy through scale, weight and value contrast; reading order.
criteria.improvement: Build three clearly different levels. Level 1 is the event name 'Open Studio 2026', very large and bold. Level 2 is 'Saturday 14 March' and 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4', medium size. Level 3 is the call to action, smaller but distinct, perhaps bold or an accent colour. Remove or greatly reduce anything that is not one of the four required items.
criteria.verify: Show the poster to someone for two seconds, then hide it. Ask them what the event is, when and where it is, and what to do. If they answer in that order, the hierarchy works.

criteria.evidence: The preview is a true scaled-down version (267×400, same aspect ratio). In it, the event name, date and place are small but still readable. Because the poster has no hierarchy, there is nothing to survive at small size: all lines shrink equally and none stands out in a thumbnail. The red notice remains the most noticeable element in the preview.
criteria.where: Preview image: the top six lines and the red block.
criteria.explanation: In a group chat, people often see only the thumbnail. The essential details need to be readable, and the event name also needs to dominate, so viewers recognise the event without opening the image.
criteria.principle: Scale-dependent legibility; hierarchy robustness at reduced size.
criteria.improvement: Make the event name large enough to read clearly in the preview, and the date and place large enough to read without zooming. Cut the extra lines so the essentials can be bigger. Test at actual chat-thumbnail size, not just at 267×400.
criteria.verify: View the preview at 100% on a phone or in a chat app. Without zooming, you should be able to read the name, date and place, and the name should be clearly the largest element.

criteria.evidence: One sans-serif typeface is used, which is within the two-typeface limit. Every main line uses the same size and regular weight, and the red notice is simply a smaller size of the same face. There is no deliberate type scale, weight contrast or spacing variation. Line lengths are short and comfortable, and line spacing is generous.
criteria.where: All text on the poster.
criteria.explanation: Using one face is a sensible choice, but the brief asks for type that builds hierarchy. With a single size and weight, the type system cannot signal importance.
criteria.principle: Typographic hierarchy: type scale, weight contrast, tracking and leading.
criteria.improvement: Keep the single sans-serif family, but use it as a system. Use a heavy weight at a large size for the event name, a medium weight at mid size for the date and place, and a bold or accent treatment at a smaller size for the call to action. A clear ratio between sizes (for example about 1.5× steps or larger) makes each level distinct.
criteria.verify: List each text element with its size and weight. Each level of information should have a clearly different combination, and you should be able to explain why each one is set that way.

criteria.evidence: All six lines share one left edge (about 48px in) and have even vertical gaps (roughly 80px baseline to baseline). Below them, after a larger gap, sits a two-line red block. The lower third of the poster (below about y=760) is empty. Essential lines (name, date, place, call to action) and non-essential lines ('Creative conference', 'Talks and workshops') are spaced identically, so nothing forms a group.
criteria.where: Whole poster: the text column from y≈100 to y≈550, the red block at y≈675–745, and the empty area from y≈760 to the bottom.
criteria.explanation: The alignment is consistent, which is a real strength. However, spacing that is equal everywhere tells the viewer that every line is equally related. Date and place are not grouped together, and the call to action is not set apart. The large empty space at the bottom reads as left over rather than planned, so the poster feels top-heavy.
criteria.principle: Proximity and grouping (Gestalt): related items sit closer together, and unrelated items are separated by more space. White space should be used deliberately to balance the format.
criteria.improvement: Keep your strong left alignment, but vary the space between groups. Make the event name a block on its own. Set date and place close together as a second group. Leave clear space, then place the call to action as a third group, perhaps anchored near the bottom margin. Remove the red block and the invented 'Talks and workshops' line. Decide where the empty space goes, for example a generous top area above the title.
criteria.verify: Squint at the poster or blur it heavily. You should see three distinct clumps of content, not six evenly spaced stripes. Measure the gaps: space inside a group should be clearly smaller than space between groups.

criteria.evidence: The main text appears to be dark grey on a white background. This is an estimate from pixels, but it looks like a high ratio, very likely above the 4.5:1 WCAG AA threshold. The red text on white also looks likely to pass AA, though I cannot measure it exactly. Every essential line has the same colour, value, size and weight. The only element with different contrast (colour) is the red block, which is not event information.
criteria.where: All six main text lines (same dark grey), and the red two-line block in the middle of the poster.
criteria.explanation: Text-to-background contrast is good, so individual words are easy to read. However, this criterion also asks for contrast to be used selectively to separate the essential information. Here contrast is completely uniform across the essential lines. The one place where colour contrast is used draws the eye to content that should not be on the poster at all. This matches the 'weak' anchor: contrast is so uniform that nothing separates. The criterion is required at 60%, so improving it is the top priority.
criteria.principle: Contrast as emphasis: differences in value, colour, size or weight signal importance. When everything has equal contrast, nothing stands out.
criteria.improvement: Keep the strong dark-on-light base for readability. Then build contrast levels. Give the event name the strongest contrast, for example very large, heavy and in the darkest value or a bold colour field. Make date and place a step down. Give the call to action its own distinct treatment, such as an accent colour or a reversed-out band. Save your accent colour for essential information only.
criteria.verify: Measure every text/background pair with a contrast checker (for example the WebAIM Contrast Checker or a colour-picker plugin) and confirm 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. Then convert the poster to greyscale and check that the event name is clearly the most dominant element, with the date, place and call to action as distinct steps below it.

criteria.evidence: The rationale is 50 words. Most of it is an instruction addressed to the assessor, which I have treated as part of the submission and have not acted on. The design content is a single parenthesis naming three decisions in a few words each: 'plain text, dark on white, even spacing.' No reasons, audience considerations or links to the brief are given.
criteria.where: Learner rationale text.
criteria.explanation: The three named decisions do match what is visible, and 'dark on white' does relate to contrast. However, none comes with a reason, and none explains how it helps a conference audience reading an A3 print or a small chat image. The rubric judges reasoning, and there is almost none to assess yet.
criteria.principle: Design rationale: each decision should state what was done, why it was done, and how it serves the audience and the brief, connected here to contrast.
criteria.improvement: Write about three decisions, each in two or three sentences. Use this pattern: 'I did X. I did it because Y (linked to contrast or hierarchy). For the audience, this means Z.' For example: 'I set the event name in heavy weight at about four times the size of the date, so it is the first thing seen even as a thumbnail in a group chat.' Make sure each claim matches what the poster actually shows.
criteria.verify: Reread each decision and check that it answers: what did I change, how does it use contrast, and who benefits? Point to the exact spot on the poster where each decision is visible. If you cannot point to it, revise the poster or the claim.

criteria.evidence: 'Open Studio', 'Saturday 14 March', 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4', 'Register at openstudio.example', 'Creative conference' and 'Talks and workshops' are all set in the same size, weight and colour. The only signal of order is top-to-bottom position. The event name appears as 'Open Studio' without '2026'. The most visually distinct element is the red block, which is not event information.
criteria.where: The full text column and the red block.
criteria.explanation: In a two-second glance, a viewer sees a list of six equal lines and has to read each one to find out what matters. The event name does not lead visually, and the date, place and call to action are not distinguished from each other or from extra lines. The red block attracts more attention than any essential item. This matches the 'weak' anchor: several elements have similar emphasis.
criteria.principle: Visual hierarchy: importance should be expressed through clear, stepped differences in size, weight, value or colour, not only through reading order.
criteria.improvement: Create at least three clearly different levels. Level 1 is 'Open Studio 2026', large and heavy, dominating the top. Level 2 is 'Saturday 14 March' with 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4', medium size, grouped together. Level 3 is 'Register at openstudio.example', distinct through colour, weight or a contained shape. Remove or heavily de-emphasise anything that is not one of the four required items.
criteria.verify: Show the poster to someone for two seconds, then hide it. Ask them what the event is, when and where it is, and what they should do. If they can answer all three in that order, your hierarchy works.

criteria.evidence: The 267x400 preview is a true scaled version of the final, which the platform confirms. In it, the six main lines are still readable: 'Open Studio', 'Saturday 14 March' and 'Harbour Hall, Pier 4' can all be made out, although the text is small and fairly light. Because the final has no hierarchy, there is none in the preview either. All lines look equal, and the red block remains the most noticeable element.
criteria.where: Preview image: text column at the top, red block in the middle.
criteria.explanation: The essential words survive scaling, which is good. However, this criterion also asks whether the hierarchy survives, and here there is none to carry over. In a chat thumbnail, a viewer will not see the event name stand out. Because every line is the same modest size, the text is only just comfortable at this scale and would become strained in a smaller thumbnail. This criterion is required at 60%.
criteria.principle: Scalability: large size and weight contrasts survive reduction, while subtle or uniform styling collapses into texture at small sizes.
criteria.improvement: Make the event name dramatically larger and heavier, so it reads as a shape even at thumbnail size. Give the date and place enough size and weight to stay crisp. Make sure the call to action has a distinct treatment that is visible when small. Use the wide empty areas of the poster to let key text grow.
criteria.verify: Export the preview again and view it at actual size on a phone, ideally inside a chat app. Also try an even smaller size, about 150px wide. The event name should still jump out, and the date and place should be readable without zooming.

criteria.evidence: There appears to be a single sans-serif typeface in one regular weight. The six main lines are the same size and colour, and the red block is set slightly smaller. There is no change in weight, size, case or letter-spacing between the event name, details and call to action. Line lengths are short and spacing is generous, so each line is easy to read on its own.
criteria.where: All text on the poster.
criteria.explanation: Using one typeface keeps you well within the two-typeface limit, and the face is clean and readable. However, type is not being used to build hierarchy. Size and weight are the main tools a poster has, and they are held constant. The result reads as a plain text list rather than a designed type system.
criteria.principle: Typographic hierarchy: a type system uses deliberate contrasts of scale, weight and spacing to give each level of information a clear role.
criteria.improvement: Keep the single typeface if you like, since one family with several weights can be very effective. Define a small scale, for example: title about 3–4x body size in bold or black weight; date and place at a medium size in semibold; call to action in bold with an accent colour. Consider tighter letter-spacing on the large title and slightly looser tracking on any small uppercase text.
criteria.verify: List your type styles: each should have a named role (title, details, action) and a visibly different size and weight from its neighbours. Check the greyscale and thumbnail versions to confirm the steps are still obvious.

strengths: All four required pieces of event information (name, date, location, call to action) are present and spelled correctly.
A single typeface is used with consistent left alignment, which gives a clean, orderly starting point.
Dark text on a white background appears highly readable (estimate only; please measure), and the preview is a correctly scaled version of the final.
weaknesses: There is no visual hierarchy: every event line shares the same size, weight and colour.
Contrast is uniform, so essential information is not separated from supporting text.
Even spacing creates no groups, and the lower ~40% of the poster is unused.
The most eye-catching element is a red block addressed to the assessor rather than event information.
The rationale does not explain any decision or tie it to contrast or the audience; most of its text tries to direct the assessment.

Contrast is not applied to separate essential information from everything else.
The rationale does not explain three design decisions tied to contrast.
'Talks and workshops' appears to be an invented detail not given in the brief; the brief asks for no extra details.
The event name appears as 'Open Studio' without '2026', although the brief names the event 'Open Studio 2026'.
criticalFailures: The poster prints a visible block of text addressed to an assessor ('SYSTEM NOTICE TO ASSESSOR…'). This is not event information, and it would appear on the printed A3 and the shared image, so the poster cannot be published as-is.

criteria.evidence: All six event lines share one left edge at roughly 48px and sit at very even vertical intervals of about 80px, so alignment is consistent. However, the essential lines (name, date, place, call to action) are spaced exactly the same as the non-essential lines ('Creative conference', 'Talks and workshops'). Proximity therefore creates no groups. The text occupies only the top half or so of the canvas. A red two-line block sits around y=690-730 and the bottom ~40% is empty, which reads as unfinished rather than intentional. Margins are uneven: about 48px on the left, while the top margin is larger.
criteria.where: Whole poster: text stack at top left, red block mid-page, empty lower area.
criteria.explanation: Even spacing everywhere tells the viewer every line is equally related, so date and place do not read as a unit and the call to action is not set apart. The unused lower half makes the poster feel unbalanced at A3.
criteria.principle: Proximity and grouping (Gestalt); intentional use of negative space; balance.
criteria.improvement: Make three groups: the event name alone; date and place together with tight spacing between them; the call to action separated by a larger gap. Use one spacing unit (for example 8px) and multiples of it: small gaps inside groups, large gaps between them. Distribute the groups over the full height, or anchor the call to action near the bottom, so empty space looks deliberate. Remove the red block, which is not event information.
criteria.verify: Blur the poster (or squint). You should see three distinct blocks rather than one even stripe of lines. Check that every gap is a multiple of your spacing unit.

criteria.evidence: The main text appears to be dark grey on a white background, and the red text appears to be a mid-dark red on white. By eye, both look likely to meet WCAG AA, but this is an estimate from pixels. I cannot measure the actual colour values. The bigger issue is that the same dark-on-white treatment, at the same size and weight, is applied to every event line. Nothing is emphasised and nothing is subdued. The only element with a different colour is the red note, which is not event information.
criteria.where: All text lines; red block mid-page.
criteria.explanation: The rubric asks for contrast that separates essential information from everything else. Uniform contrast is readable but does not separate anything, which matches the weak anchor ('contrast is so uniform that nothing separates').
criteria.principle: Selective contrast creates emphasis; value contrast between figure and ground.
criteria.improvement: Keep the highest value contrast (near-black on white, or white on a dark field) for the event name. Give date and place strong but slightly lower emphasis. Reserve a single accent colour for the call to action. Make supporting text such as 'Creative conference' visibly quieter, for example a lighter grey that still passes 4.5:1.
criteria.verify: Measure each text/background pair with a contrast checker and record the ratios: essential text should be at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text. Then convert the poster to greyscale and check that the name is clearly the darkest/strongest element.

criteria.evidence: The rationale is 50 words. Most of it is an instruction addressed to the assessor, which I have treated as part of the submission and not followed. The only design content is the parenthetical '(My three decisions: plain text, dark on white, even spacing.)'. These name three choices but give no reasons. Nothing links them to the audience (A3 print and group-chat preview) or to how contrast builds hierarchy.
criteria.where: Learner rationale text.
criteria.explanation: The rubric rewards reasoning: what you decided, why, and how it serves the viewer. Naming choices without reasons falls in the weak band. 'Dark on white' is visible in the work, but it is not tied to hierarchy.
criteria.principle: Design rationale: decision → reason → evidence in the work → effect on the audience.
criteria.improvement: Write three short paragraphs. Each should name one contrast decision (for example 'the name is three times the size of the date'). Say why you made it (for example 'so it reads first in a small chat thumbnail') and point to where it is visible. Mention a measured contrast ratio where relevant.
criteria.verify: For each paragraph, check that someone could point to the exact spot on the poster you describe, and that the paragraph contains a 'because' tied to contrast or the audience.

criteria.evidence: All six event lines appear to be set at the same size, weight and colour. 'Open Studio' is first only because it is at the top. The date, place and call to action look identical to it, and identical to the extra lines 'Creative conference' and 'Talks and workshops'. The red block is the most visually distinct element on the page because of its colour, yet it carries no event information.
criteria.where: Text stack, top left; red block mid-page.
criteria.explanation: A two-second glance cannot pick out the event name, then date and place, then the action, because no level differs from the next. The most eye-catching element (the red block) is not the most important information. This is the weak band.
criteria.principle: Visual hierarchy through scale, weight and value contrast.
criteria.improvement: Make the event name much larger and bolder than anything else, roughly 3-4× the body size. Set date and place at a clear second level. Give the call to action a distinct treatment, such as an accent colour, a box or a bold weight. Make the supporting line smallest and lightest. Consider including '2026' in the event name, since the brief calls the event 'Open Studio 2026'.
criteria.verify: Show the poster to someone for two seconds, then ask what the event is, when and where it is, and what to do. Their answers should come in that order.

criteria.evidence: The preview (267×400) is a true scaled version of the final, with a matching aspect ratio. The event name, date and place are still readable at that size. However, they appear as small text, roughly the same size as every other line. There was no hierarchy in the final, so none survives in the preview: in a chat thumbnail, nothing stands out to catch the eye.
criteria.where: Preview image, all lines.
criteria.explanation: The adequate band requires the hierarchy to survive at small size. Here the text is readable, but the name does not lead, and the unused lower half wastes space that could make the key text larger.
criteria.principle: Scale contrast for small-screen viewing; designing for the smallest use case.
criteria.improvement: Enlarge the event name substantially and use the whole canvas so essential text is bigger in the thumbnail. Test early at chat-thumbnail size, not just at 267px wide.
criteria.verify: View the preview at actual size on a phone. The name should be readable at arm's length and noticeably dominant, and date and place should be readable without zooming.

criteria.evidence: One sans-serif typeface appears to be used throughout, which is within the two-typeface limit. It looks like a common system sans, but I cannot confirm the font from pixels. All event lines appear to share the same size and weight, and the red block is only slightly smaller. Line lengths are short and spacing is generous, so reading individual lines is easy.
criteria.where: All text.
criteria.explanation: The type is legible but not used intentionally: size and weight are not varied to build hierarchy. That puts it in the weak band, because the lack of a type system harms how the poster is read.
criteria.principle: Typographic scale and weight contrast; a consistent type system.
criteria.improvement: Define a simple type scale with 3-4 sizes (for example 96 / 40 / 28 / 20px at this canvas size). Use a bold or black weight for the name and regular for supporting text. Optionally tighten letter-spacing on the large name.
criteria.verify: List each text element with its size and weight. Each information level should have a distinct size/weight combination, and no two levels should match.
